How NoCharge builds current puzzle starts

An implementation-level look at deterministic Lights Out and Minesweeper, formula-derived Nonogram clues, fixed Sudoku boards, and the limits of those methods.

By NoCharge Editorial·Reviewed by NoCharge Editorial·Published August 27, 2026·Updated November 24, 2026·2 min read

Bottom line: Current NoCharge puzzles do not all use one generator. Some starts are fixed, some are derived from a deterministic rule, and some use a seeded sequence. This article describes those implementations without claiming that every puzzle is random, solver-verified, or uniquely solvable.

Lights Out: reversible seeded toggles

The five-by-five board starts all off. The game applies 13 cross-shaped presses selected from a seeded sequence. Since each press is its own inverse, applying the same presses can return the board to all off. That proves a solution exists; it does not prove uniqueness or a shortest move count.

Minesweeper: lay mines after the first choice

The nine-by-nine board contains ten mines. The mine layout is created on the first reveal with a deterministic seed and excludes that selected square, so the first revealed cell is safe. The source does not protect the eight neighboring cells as a group.

Nonogram: derive clues from a formula

The current Nonogram offers 5×5 and 10×10 sizes. A distance-from-center rule creates the filled-cell pattern for each size, and row and column run clues are derived from that pattern. This is not a library of 24 hand-curated puzzles, and the current source does not claim a separate uniqueness-verification pass.

Sudoku: fixed boards, not a runtime generator

Mini Sudoku and Sudoku 9×9 initialize fixed starting grids and bundled solutions. The current source does not build a new grid by removing clues and running a solver, nor does it offer the old easy/medium/hard given-count selector. The interface checks row, column, and box entries against its current puzzle.

Other reproducible starts

Beacon Lattice begins with an empty 5×5 board and the same five F, V, I, U, and L pentominoes; it does not load a solver-backed pack of locked obstacles. Word Search starts from a deterministic 8×8 grid with four fixed word placements. Memory Match and several other games also use seeded initial state, so reset may restore the same arrangement rather than create a fresh random board.

What these statements do not prove

A reproducible start is not automatically a unique solution, an appropriate difficulty, or a guarantee about enjoyment. The current game page is the source for the live controls and rules. These implementation notes are not a cognitive-benefit claim or a promise that every possible input/device combination has been tested.
